Carl Friedrich Gauss. A German mathematician and astronomer from seventeen seventy-seven to eighteen fifty-five, often called the Prince of Mathematicians for his extraordinary contributions spanning number theory, statistics, algebra, analysis, and geometry.

He proved the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: every polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots in the complex numbers, counting multiplicity. This was a major breakthrough that showed the completeness of the complex number system. He worked extensively with Gaussian integers, complex numbers of the form a plus bi where a and b are integers. These have unique factorisation properties, extending the concept of prime factorisation into the complex plane. His Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, published in eighteen hundred one, is the foundational modern text on number theory. It introduced modular arithmetic and the rigorous study of quadratic residues, establishing number theory as a systematic discipline.

The normal distribution, the bell curve, is also called the Gaussian distribution. Gauss developed the method of least squares for fitting data to curves, which became the standard method in all empirical science. He demonstrated its power by computing the orbit of the asteroid Ceres using incomplete observations—a remarkable feat of prediction that showed how even limited data can yield accurate results when the right mathematical techniques are applied. This was a stunning demonstration of the practical power of mathematics.

He developed the concept of Gaussian curvature, the intrinsic curvature of a surface, and realised that space need not be Euclidean. This was a crucial step toward non-Euclidean geometry, and he explored curved spaces privately, predating the public discovery of hyperbolic geometry. The Divergence Theorem, also known as Gauss's Theorem, relates the flux of a vector field through a closed surface to the divergence of the field inside, connecting local and global properties of vector fields.

Gauss was a colossus of nineteenth-century mathematics. His work in number theory reframed the discipline, his statistical methods became indispensable in all empirical science, and his geometric intuition presaged Einstein's curved spacetime. Yet he published conservatively, obsessed with perfection. Many of his most important discoveries sat in his private notebooks for decades, their significance unrecognised until after his death. This secrecy may have slowed some fields—non-Euclidean geometry might have developed faster if his private work had been public—but whenever his work finally appeared, it was pristine and influential. His legacy is woven into the fabric of modern science: the bell curve in statistics, the normal equations in machine learning, the curvature tensor in relativity. All bear his mark.
